results.title: Integrated system modeling in SysML for small satellites
results.abstract: Small satellites (>100kg) are becoming more prevalent with increasing mission types driving the complexity of the design. These missions range from earth imaging to technological demonstrations as well as educational uses within universities. The design and engineering of these satellites become more challenging with the miniature size, coupled subsystems and dynamic environments. One major issue of this architecture is the selection and verification of requirements. Model-based systems engineering is a powerful system engineering methodology providing engineers a model of the entire system model. This modeling environment can provide system design in the trade space as well as integrating disciplines together and allowing simulation. NASA Marshall Space Flight Center is currently working on a small satellite using an iodine fueled Hall thruster, called iSAT. This 12U satellite will be a technological demonstration of the use of a 200W Hall thruster in low earth orbit. Integrating the system models into SysML with the requirements and system architecture allowed for an analysis of the power system. A simulation of the power system was completed providing insight into the design.
results.publicationTitle: AIAA Modeling and Simulation Technologies Conference 2017

results.title: Open-source CubeSat MBSE Approach to Address Traceability: Power Subsystem
results.abstract: The benefits of using Model-based System Engineering (MBSE) approaches for the development of projects go beyond just replacing document-centric methods. MBSE is expected to aid in the ability to manage complexity and capture knowledge. By using MBSE approaches on CubeSats this paper aims to address notions of traceability and how system models can be used to verify the fulfillment of requirements. This work is carried out in Papyrus, an open-source model-based engineering tool, and builds on existing studies regarding CubeSats system models. The development of these sorts of models can benefit future CubeSat developers by reducing design time and cost. These models can also be used in an academic setting to facilitate learning about CubeSats and their design process. In this paper, a CubeSat power subsystem SysML model is presented, while the notion of traceability is introduced by the creation of a specific profile for model assumptions and a java code that allows visualizing the impacts of the change of one or more parameters of the CubeSat model. The model proposed in this paper contains key information about a system, such as requirements, structure, behavior, and analysis. This model-based approach for CubeSat subsystems helps to visualize and understand what is needed for the design of a CubeSat power subsystem, while guaranteeing that the designers are clearly aware of which requirements are being met and which are not.

results.title: 6S CubeSat: a Student-made IOD Mission for Characterization of Perovskite Solar Cells and Structural Battery
results.abstract: The 6S CubeSat mission is the flagship project of the university student association PoliSpace which aims to design, manufacture, and operate the first student-made 1U CubeSat of Politecnico di Milano. Moreover, since January 2023, the project has been part of the pilot edition of ESA's “Fly Your Satellite! Design Booster” program aiming to support selected teams through the consolidation of the design by arranging regular reviews with ESA experts. Looking at potential improvements in space technology and its transfer, 6S CubeSat was developed as a technological demonstrator of two payloads focused on in-orbit power production and storage; Volta structural battery and PErovskite Solar Cells Analyzer (PESCA). The former is a game-changing concept that combines both form and function, aiming to significantly reduce weight and complexity in satellite design. The latter, instead, will manage the testing of Perovskite solar cells, which promise high efficiency, high power-to-mass ratio, low production cost, and excellent resistance to radiation, making them a good alternative to Silicon-based Solar Cells, both for terrestrial and in-space applications. Furthermore, a derived goal from PESCA is to develop and validate an open-source, affordable, and highly effective solar cells testing platform built in-house. Along with 6S' second in-house component, the CubeSat structure, these two present the main challenges of the CubeSat construction and qualification. Students from BSc, MSc, and PhD careers are organized in teams that include Attitude and Orbit Control System, Electrical Power System, Mission Analysis, Payload, On-Board Data Handling and Flight Software, Thermal Control System, Telemetry and Telecommand, System Engineers, and Structural teams that translate the theoretical background provided by the university courses of diverse backgrounds to the application of standard practices in space mission design. This also involves the adoption of ECSS and SAVOIR standards and practices of Model Based System Engineering, targeting a high academic return for the students involved. The paper aims to present the technological and educational mission objectives. Additionally, it will provide a complete overview of the mission baseline by detailing the technical design choices and relevant results achieved by the teams cooperating in the project.

results.title: CONCURRENT ENGINEERING PROCESS FOR ELECTRICAL ARCHITECTURE OF NANOSATELLITES PRELIMINARY PHASES
results.abstract: The transformation and evolution of the space sector relies on technological innovation, but also on digital transformation. The increasing complexity of space systems led to the deployment of new digital solutions and methodologies such as Model-Based Systems Engineering that helps to better comprehend this complexity on an individual scale. This leads to new ways of approaching projects, such as concurrent engineering which consists in involving all project stakeholders right from the preliminary phases, using facilitating tools and methods. At CNES, PASO (Orbital Systems Architecture Plateau) is leading space systems preliminary phases and aims at formulating missions needs and pre-sizing systems in order to conclude on their feasibility. This process is conducted accordingly to the principles of concurrent engineering, thus involving all systems architects and thematic experts from the very beginning of the projects. The objective of this paper is to describe the approach through the prism of an electrical architect, that contributes to needs analysis, realization of power budgets, system sizing and energetic simulations through a specific use case. All this is achieved thanks to a precise workflow involving multiple digital tools, with continuity and interoperability made possible between engineers and their tools by the standardization of formats and files.

results.title: Preliminary Design of the JETSON-Low Power Spacecraft
results.abstract: The Joint Emergent Technology Supplying On-orbit Nuclear (JETSON) Low Power (LP) project has completed the key milestone of a successful Preliminary Design Review (PDR) in September 2025. Commencing with contract award by the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) Space Vehicles Directorate (RV) in September 2023, a team led by Intuitive Machines (IM) achieved three goals established for the project. First was development of a power system capable of creating at least 20We using Stirling cycle-based dynamic power conversion technology powered by a novel (non-Pu-238) Radioisotope Power System (RPS) Heat Source (HS). During the first of three Design Analysis Cycles (DACs), a comprehensive trade study was performed which examined the following novel nuclear heat sources: Am-241, Co-60, Sr-90, and U-235. Co-60 was selected primarily based on cost-effective commercial availability to meet the goal of a March 2029 launch date target. Because of the challenges of handling such a strong gamma emitter, radiation shielding and handling were a major focus for the JETSON-LP design, which was subsequently matured in DACs 2 and 3. The second goal was to explore the design space for RPS-based spacecraft, resulting in a SmallSat spacecraft preliminary design. This goal included developing maturation plans for the following five Critical Technology Elements (CTEs): the RPS Heat Source, Thermal Control Radiators, Radiation Shielding, Power Conversion/Management, and Propulsion Systems. The final primary goal was development of a Model Based System Engineering (MBSE) model of the JETSON-LP system and assessment of other critical systems engineering and integration aspects. These included working closely with AFRL to develop an integrated Cameo and Simulink/SimScape model, carefully analyzing a launch approval process in accordance with the Interagency Nuclear Safety Review Board (INSRB), National Environmental Protection Act (NEPA), and Department of Air Force (DAF) range safety requirements, and investigating several launch options, considering multiple launch vehicles with the JETSON-LP spacecraft riding into orbit as both a primary and a ride-along payload.
